candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — breastfeeding and return to work
candidate.educational_objective: Teach milk-expression frequency that supports continued lactation during separation and accurately describe current U.S. workplace pumping protections.

options.A: Express milk about as often as the infant normally drinks breast milk while they are apart.
options.B: Stop breastfeeding after returning to work because pumping cannot support milk production.
options.C: Expect milk production to fall sharply whenever daytime separation begins, regardless of milk removal.
options.D: Avoid discussing workplace pumping because federal protections never apply to nursing employees.

candidate.rationale: CDC guidance updated in 2026 advises people who are away from their baby to pump about as often as the baby normally drinks breast milk; regular milk removal helps the body continue making the amount of milk the baby needs. Most covered U.S. employees also have federal rights to reasonable pump breaks and a private non-bathroom space for up to one year after birth, subject to statutory coverage and exemptions. A is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: When separated from the infant, pump about as often as the baby normally drinks breast milk to help maintain supply; most covered employees have reasonable-break and private-space protections for pumping at work.
candidate.source_document_title: Breastfeeding and Returning to Your Workplace; Pumping Breast Milk; FLSA Protections to Pump at Work
candidate.source_locator: CDC — How often to pump/return-to-work considerations; DOL — What You Should Know
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); U.S. Department of Labor (DOL)
candidate.source_version_date: CDC March 13, 2026 and February 24, 2026; DOL revised January 2026
candidate.stem: A breastfeeding client is returning to work and wants to maintain milk production while separated from the infant. Which teaching is most appropriate?
